dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: Why do many linked-list implementations start with a dummy (sentinel) head node?
options: It lets the garbage collector free nodes sooner
It makes the list doubly linked without extra pointers
It speeds up random access to the middle of the list
It removes special cases for inserting or deleting at the front, since every real node then has a predecessor
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: With a sentinel, the 'previous node' always exists, so deleting the first real node is the same code path as deleting any other (prev.next = prev.next.next). It does nothing for random access, which stays O(n), and has no effect on garbage collection.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: An LRU cache combines a Map (key to node) with a doubly linked list. Why doubly rather than singly linked?
options: Doubly linked lists use less memory per node
Given a node from the Map, it can be unlinked in O(1) using its prev pointer; a singly linked list must search for the predecessor in O(n)
Map entries can only reference doubly linked nodes
It keeps keys sorted for range queries
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: On a cache hit you jump straight to the node through the Map and move it to the front. Unlinking requires changing the predecessor's next pointer, which a prev pointer gives you in O(1). A singly linked list would have to walk from the head. The trade-off is one extra pointer per node, so more memory, not less.

Each unshift creates a new head that points to the old head, so the last value inserted is first: 3->2->1, and size counts three insertions. Inserting at the head is O(1); keeping insertion order would need a tail pointer.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: What's wrong with this `remove(val)` method on a singly linked list with a `head` field and no sentinel?
options: It never checks the head node itself, and it throws a TypeError on an empty list
It leaks the removed node because it doesn't set node.next = null
It runs in O(n^2) because of the nested property access
It removes every matching node instead of the first one
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: The loop only ever inspects cur.next, so a match at the head is never removed. When head is null, reading cur.next throws. A sentinel head, or an explicit head check, fixes both. Removed nodes become unreachable and are garbage collected, so there's no leak.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: A doubly linked list class's `remove(node)` fixes the prev/next pointers but never updates `this.tail` when the removed node is the tail. After removing the tail and then calling `push(x)`, what happens?
options: Nothing; push walks from head to find the real last node
x replaces the head node
push throws because tail is null
x is linked after the removed node, so a traversal from head never reaches it
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: push typically does tail.next = node and node.prev = tail. A stale tail still points at the detached node, so x hangs off a node that is no longer reachable from head. The list silently loses data and its size goes out of sync. tail isn't null, so nothing throws.

Unlinking b points a.next at c and c.prev at a, so both directions skip b: forward 'ac', backward 'ca'. b's own pointers are untouched, so b.next is still c. That's harmless here, but a stale pointer can be a bug if someone keeps using b.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: What is the time complexity of `get(i)` (the value at index i) in a singly linked list of n nodes?
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(i), which is O(n) in the worst case
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: There is no index arithmetic: you follow next pointers i times from the head. Arrays give O(1) access because elements sit at computable addresses. A doubly linked list can start from whichever end is closer, but the worst case is still O(n).

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: When is a linked list a better choice than a plain JavaScript array? Select all that apply.
options: Moving a run of nodes between lists in O(1) when you hold its ends
Removing an arbitrary node in O(1) when you already hold a reference to it (e.g. an LRU cache)
A FIFO queue that must dequeue from the front in O(1) without index tricks
Frequent random access by index
Tight loops where CPU cache-friendly iteration matters most
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: Linked lists are good at O(1) splicing around nodes you already hold. They are bad at indexing (O(n)), and their scattered nodes iterate more slowly than contiguous arrays because of cache misses. That's why arrays win most 'just iterate' workloads in practice.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: You insert node x after node p in a doubly linked list, where p is not the tail. Which assignments are required? Select all that apply.
options: head = x
x.prev = p
x.next = p.next
p.next.prev = x
p.next = x (done after p.next.prev is updated)
p.prev = x
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: x needs both of its links, and both neighbours must point back at x. Order matters: update p.next.prev before overwriting p.next, or you lose the reference to the old successor. p.prev and head are unaffected by inserting after p.

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: In JavaScript, a node removed from a linked list must be explicitly freed, or it will leak memory.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: False. JS is garbage collected: once nothing references the node it is reclaimed. Leaks happen only if something still holds it, such as a stale Map entry or a forgotten tail pointer. Setting node.next = null can help in rare cases, but there's no free().

dsa-lists-trees:0.prompt: With both head and tail pointers, a singly linked list can append in O(1), but removing the tail still takes O(n).
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:0.explanation: True. Appending only touches tail.next and tail. Removing the tail means the new tail is its predecessor, and a singly linked list can only find that by walking from the head. That's why deques and LRU caches use doubly linked lists.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: In Floyd's cycle detection (slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2), why must the pointers meet if there's a cycle?
options: The cycle length is always even
Slow stops moving once it enters the cycle
Fast eventually laps the whole list and resets to head
Once both are in the cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 each step, so it reaches 0 instead of jumping over it
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: Inside the cycle, fast gains one node per step, so the distance from fast back to slow decreases by 1 every iteration and hits 0. Fast can't skip over slow. Nothing depends on the cycle length being even.

Reversal reuses the same nodes. r is the old tail and walks 4321. h still points at node 1, which is now the last node with next = null, so it prints just '1'. Expecting h to still read 1234 assumes a copy was made.

With `while (f && f.next)`, slow stops at the exact middle of an odd-length list and at the second of the two middles of an even-length list (3 for [1,2,3,4]). To get the first middle, loop on `f.next && f.next.next` instead.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet inside a cycle, you reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time. Why do they next meet at the cycle's entry node?
options: Because slow has traversed the cycle exactly once
Because the meeting point is always the node just before the entry
Because the distance from head to the entry is congruent (mod cycle length) to the distance from the meeting point forward to the entry
Because the cycle length equals the tail length
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: If the tail has length μ and the cycle length L, then at the meeting point 2(μ + k) ≡ μ + k (mod L), so μ + k ≡ 0 and the meeting point is μ steps (mod L) short of the entry. Walking μ steps from head and from the meeting point lands both on the entry. The tail and cycle lengths needn't be equal.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: To remove the n-th node from the end in one pass, fast is advanced n steps, then fast and slow move together. Why start both at a dummy node before head?
options: It makes the algorithm O(1) instead of O(n)
If the node to remove is the head itself, slow still has a predecessor to unlink from, so there's no special case
It prevents fast from ever becoming null
It's required for lists with an even length
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: Removal needs the node before the target. When n equals the list length, the target is head, which has no real predecessor; the dummy provides one, and you return dummy.next. The algorithm is O(L) either way.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: A palindrome-list check finds the middle, reverses the second half in place, compares the halves, and returns. In code review, what's the most valid concern?
options: It mutates the caller's list; it should reverse the second half back before returning, or document the side effect
It fails for odd-length lists because the middle node is compared with itself
It needs O(n) extra space for the reversed half
It's O(n^2) because reversal is O(n) per comparison
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: The point of the trick is O(1) extra space, but it rewires the input. Other code holding the list now sees it broken after the midpoint. Restoring the half (one more O(n) reversal) fixes that. The time is O(n), and odd lengths work if the middle is skipped.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: A recursive linked-list reversal works in tests but fails in production on a 200,000-node list in Node.js. What's the most likely error?
options: Out-of-memory in the heap because each node is copied
An infinite loop because recursion revisits nodes
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, since V8 doesn't do tail-call optimization
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: Recursion depth equals the list length, and V8 doesn't eliminate tail calls, so roughly 10k+ frames (depending on frame size) overflow the stack. The iterative three-pointer version uses O(1) space. Nodes aren't copied, so heap memory isn't the problem.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: Which problems are typically solved with fast/slow pointers? Select all that apply.
options: Happy number (does repeated digit-square-sum reach 1?)
Merging two sorted linked lists
Detecting a cycle in a linked list
Finding the middle node in one pass
Finding the duplicate in an array of n+1 values in 1..n without modifying it, using O(1) space
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: The duplicate-number problem treats i → nums[i] as a linked list with a cycle, and happy numbers either reach 1 or cycle; Floyd finds both in O(1) space. Merging two sorted lists uses two pointers, one in each list, but not a fast/slow pair.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: Which statements about iterative in-place reversal of a singly linked list are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space
You must save head.next before overwriting head.next
It returns the old tail as the new head
It requires a doubly linked list
Afterwards the old head pointer still lets you traverse the whole reversed list
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: Three pointers (prev, cur, next) make it O(n) time and O(1) space. Without saving next first you lose the rest of the list. The old head becomes the tail, so traversing from it shows a single node. Only next pointers are needed, so no doubly linked list.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: Floyd's algorithm only works if fast moves exactly 2 steps; if fast moved 3 steps per iteration, the pointers could miss each other forever in some cycles.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: False. Both start at head, so after t steps they're at positions t and 3t. Once t is at least the tail length, they coincide whenever the cycle length divides 2t, e.g. when t is a multiple of the cycle length. Step 2 is standard because it does the least work and keeps the cycle-entry proof simple.

dsa-lists-trees:1.prompt: Floyd's cycle detection uses O(1) extra space, whereas detecting a cycle with a Set of visited nodes uses O(n).
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:1.explanation: True. Floyd's needs only two pointers. The Set approach stores every node it visits until it sees a repeat, so it uses O(n) memory. Both run in O(n) time; interviewers often ask for the O(1)-space version as a follow-up.

dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: The position of the visit relative to the two recursive calls decides the order. Preorder visits the node first (1,2,4,5,3), inorder between its subtrees (4,2,5,1,3), postorder after both (4,5,2,3,1). 12345 is level order, not preorder.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: This 'iterative preorder' pushes the left child before the right. What does it print?
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: A stack is LIFO, so the last child pushed is visited first. Pushing left then right visits the right subtree first, giving root-right-left: 1,3,2,5,4. For real preorder, push the right child first. Reversing this root-right-left order is a common trick for postorder.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in ascending order?
options: Inorder
Postorder
Level order
Preorder
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller keys), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger keys), so a BST comes out sorted. Preorder lists the root first, which is useful for copying or serializing the tree but isn't sorted.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: In iterative inorder traversal (`while (cur || stack.length)`), after popping a node and visiting it, what should the loop do next?
options: Push both children, right first
Set cur = null and pop again
Push the node's left child
Set cur = node.right, so the next iteration pushes that subtree's left spine
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: The pattern is: push the whole left spine, pop and visit, then move to the right child and repeat. The left subtree has already been handled by the time you pop. Pushing both children turns it into preorder-style processing.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: You must compute each node's subtree height (or free a tree bottom-up). Which traversal fits naturally?
options: Level order, because it processes nodes by depth
Preorder, because the root is processed first
Inorder, because it visits nodes in sorted order
Postorder, because both children's results are available before their parent is processed
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), so the children must be finished first, which is what postorder guarantees. Preorder processes the parent before its children are known. Level order runs top-down, which is backwards for this.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: Morris inorder traversal achieves O(1) extra space. What's its main trade-off?
options: It runs in O(n log n) time
It temporarily rewires right pointers to inorder predecessors, so the tree is mutated during the walk and is unsafe for concurrent readers
It only works on complete binary trees
It visits nodes in a different order from recursive inorder
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Morris threads the predecessor's right pointer back to the current node to find its way back up, then removes the thread. It's still O(n) time and produces normal inorder, but the tree is modified mid-traversal, which breaks shared or read-only structures.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: What's the extra-space complexity of recursive inorder traversal on a balanced tree versus a completely skewed tree (n nodes)?
options: O(log n) and O(n)
O(n) and O(n)
O(log n) and O(log n)
O(1) and O(1)
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Stack depth equals tree height h: about log n when balanced and n when skewed (a linked list in disguise). This is why deep, unbalanced trees can overflow the call stack in Node, and an explicit stack (stored on the heap) is safer.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: Assuming all values are distinct, which pairs of traversal sequences determine a unique binary tree? Select all that apply.
options: Level order + inorder
Inorder alone
Level order alone
Preorder + inorder
Postorder + inorder
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Inorder tells you which values fall left and right of a root, and preorder, postorder or level order tells you which value is the root. Inorder alone can't tell different shapes apart, and level order alone doesn't record which child slots are empty.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: Which tree problems are naturally solved with a postorder (children first) traversal? Select all that apply.
options: Serializing a tree so it can be rebuilt by reading tokens left to right
Height of a tree
Diameter of a binary tree
Checking whether a tree is height-balanced
Printing BST keys in ascending order
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: Height, diameter and balance all combine results from the left and right subtrees, so the children must be finished first. Sorted output is inorder. Serialization is usually preorder with null markers, because the root must come first for left-to-right rebuilding.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: Reversing a root-right-left traversal produces a postorder (left-right-root) traversal.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: True. Reversing root-right-left gives left-right-root, which is postorder. That's why a simple iterative postorder runs a modified preorder (pushing the left child before the right) and reverses the output, avoiding the trickier single-stack postorder bookkeeping.

dsa-lists-trees:2.prompt: When all values are distinct, preorder and postorder sequences together always determine a unique binary tree.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:2.explanation: False. A root with only a left child and a root with only a right child have the same preorder (root, child) and the same postorder (child, root). Preorder plus postorder is only enough for full binary trees, where every node has 0 or 2 children.

dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: Each loop iteration replaces q with all children of the current level, so the levels are [1], [2,3], [4,5]. Nodes 4 and 5 have different parents but the same depth, so they share a level. Building a fresh array per level avoids the O(n) cost of shift().

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: In queue-based level order, why do we read `const size = queue.length` at the start of each level and loop exactly `size` times?
options: To avoid an infinite loop when the tree has a cycle
So that only the nodes of the current level are processed, while children enqueued during the loop wait for the next level
Because queue.length is expensive to read inside the loop
To process the level from right to left
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: Children are appended to the same queue while you dequeue, so the queue length keeps changing. Fixing the count at the start draws the boundary between levels, which you need for per-level output, averages and right-side view. Trees have no cycles, so that isn't the reason.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: 'Binary tree right side view' returns the nodes visible from the right. With level-order BFS, which node do you record per level?
options: The last node dequeued in each level (children enqueued left before right)
The node with the largest value in each level
The rightmost leaf of the whole tree
The first node dequeued in each level
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: If children are enqueued left then right, the last node in each level is the rightmost one, even if it's a left child because there's no right sibling. Choosing the largest value is a different problem (largest value in each row).

Zigzag reverses only the output of every second level; the traversal itself stays left to right. Level 0 prints 1, level 1 prints reversed (3,2), level 2 goes back to left to right (4,5). reverse() mutates vals, which is safe because vals is a fresh array.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: To find the minimum depth of a very unbalanced binary tree (a deep left chain, plus a leaf at depth 2 on the right), why is BFS preferable to DFS?
options: DFS can't compute minimum depth correctly
BFS avoids recursion, which is the only source of cost
BFS uses less memory in all cases
BFS can stop at the first leaf it dequeues, which is the shallowest, without exploring the deep chain
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: Level order reaches leaves in order of depth, so the first leaf found is the answer and BFS stops there. A plain DFS must explore every path, including the deep chain, to be sure. DFS is still correct, just slower here, and BFS can use more memory on wide trees.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: For a complete binary tree with about 1,000,000 nodes, compare the peak extra memory of BFS (queue) and recursive DFS (call stack).
options: Both about 1,000,000 entries
Both about 20 entries
BFS about 500,000 entries (the last level); DFS about 20 frames (the height)
BFS about 20 entries; DFS about 500,000 frames
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: BFS holds a whole level, and the last level of a complete tree contains about half the nodes. DFS only holds the current root-to-node path, about log2(10^6) ≈ 20 frames. For a skewed tree the comparison flips: the queue stays tiny and DFS depth becomes n.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: In a perfect binary tree, you must set each node's `next` pointer to its right neighbour on the same level using O(1) extra space (no queue). What's the key idea?
options: Use recursion, since the call stack doesn't count as extra space
Walk each level using the next pointers already set on that level, and wire the level below: node.left.next = node.right; node.right.next = node.next?.left
Do an inorder traversal and link consecutive nodes
Store each level in an array and link neighbours
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: Once a level is linked, it acts as a linked list you can walk without a queue, and from it you connect the children, including across parents through node.next. Recursion uses O(h) stack, and an array per level is O(width) space, so neither meets the constraint.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: Which problems are naturally solved with level-order BFS on a binary tree? Select all that apply.
options: Largest value in each row
Minimum depth of the tree
k-th smallest key in a BST
Lowest common ancestor in a BST
Average value of the nodes on each level
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: Per-level aggregates and 'first leaf by depth' fit BFS directly. The k-th smallest key is an inorder walk that stops early, and LCA in a BST is a single root-to-node walk using key comparisons.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: Which statements about level-order BFS on a binary tree with n nodes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It requires parent pointers on every node
Using an array as a stack (pop) instead of a queue still yields level order
Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, so time is O(n)
Nodes are dequeued in non-decreasing order of depth
Peak queue size is proportional to the tree's maximum width
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: FIFO order makes BFS process depth d entirely before depth d+1, the queue holds at most about one level plus part of the next, and the total work is O(n). Parent pointers aren't needed. Swapping the queue for a stack turns the traversal into DFS.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: A binary tree is complete if and only if, in a BFS that also enqueues null children, no non-null node appears after the first null.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: True. A complete tree fills every level left to right with no gaps, so in level order the nulls must all come after the real nodes. A real node after a null means there's a gap, so the tree isn't complete.

dsa-lists-trees:3.prompt: Level-order traversal of a binary search tree outputs its keys in sorted order.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:3.explanation: False. Level order lists the root first, though it's usually somewhere in the middle of the sorted order. For the BST 2(1,3), level order gives 2,1,3. Only inorder produces sorted output.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, …, 10,000 in order into a plain (unbalanced) BST, then search for 10,000. What's the cost of that search?
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: Inserting sorted keys makes every new node a right child, so the tree degenerates into a chain of height n, and a search costs O(h) = O(n). O(log n) only holds for balanced trees, which is why AVL and red-black trees exist.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: Deleting a BST node that has two children: what's the standard approach?
options: Delete the node and attach both subtrees to its parent
Replace its key with its inorder successor (the minimum of the right subtree), then delete that successor, which has at most a right child
Replace it with its left child and re-insert the right subtree
Rebuild the whole tree from an inorder traversal
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: The inorder successor is the smallest key greater than the node, so putting it in the node's place preserves BST order. The successor has no left child (otherwise that child would be smaller), so deleting it is the easy case. A parent can't take two extra subtrees in one child slot.

Inserting the median first (4, then 2 and 6, and so on) builds a perfect tree of height 3. Sorted insertion turns every node into a right child, giving a chain of height 7. Same keys, different shape: a BST's shape depends on insertion order.

Iterative inorder visits keys in ascending order and stops at the k-th visit: the 3rd is 3 and the 7th is 7. For k = 8 the traversal ends first and the function returns its explicit null. Stopping early makes this O(h + k) rather than O(n).

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: What's the efficient way to find the lowest common ancestor of nodes p and q in a BST?
options: Walk from the root: go left if both keys are smaller than the node, right if both are larger, and otherwise the current node is the LCA
Do a level-order BFS and return the first node that is an ancestor of both
Return the parent of whichever node is deeper
Find both root-to-node paths with DFS and compare them
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: BST order tells you which side each key is on. The first node where p and q split (or which equals one of them) is the LCA, found in O(h) with O(1) space. Path comparison works for any binary tree but doesn't use BST order.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: In a BST without parent pointers, node x has no right child. Where is its inorder successor?
options: There's no successor; x must be the maximum
It's the leftmost node of the whole tree
It's x's left child
It's the nearest ancestor of x whose left subtree contains x (found by walking down from the root)
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: With no right subtree, the next larger key is the first ancestor you reached by going left. Walking from the root, record a candidate each time you go left. If x has a right child, the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree instead. x is the maximum only if no such ancestor exists.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: You need floor(x), the largest key ≤ x, in a BST. Which walk is correct?
options: Do an inorder traversal and return the first key ≥ x
If node.v > x go right; otherwise record node.v and go left
If node.v === x return it; if node.v > x go left; otherwise record node.v as a candidate and go right
Go left until null and return the last key seen
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: A key greater than x can't be the floor, so go left. A key smaller than x is a candidate, but a larger valid one might be in its right subtree, so record it and go right. This is O(h). Returning the first key ≥ x computes the ceiling, not the floor.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: Which properties hold for every valid BST with distinct keys? Select all that apply.
options: Inorder traversal is strictly increasing
The minimum key is in the leftmost node (keep following left children)
Every key in the left subtree of a node is smaller than that node's key
The height is O(log n)
Level-order traversal is sorted
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: BST order applies to entire subtrees, which gives sorted inorder output and a leftmost minimum. Height is only O(log n) for balanced trees; sorted insertion gives height n. Level order isn't sorted.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: For 'sum of BST keys in the range [lo, hi]', which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If node.v > hi, the right subtree can be skipped entirely
With pruning, the work is roughly O(h + k), where k is the number of keys in range
You must visit every node, because a BST doesn't store subtree sums
If node.v < lo, the left subtree can be skipped entirely
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: Everything in the left subtree is smaller than a node already below lo, so it can be skipped; the same goes for the right subtree above hi. Pruning means you only walk the two boundary paths plus the in-range nodes, so visiting every node is unnecessary.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: When deleting a node with two children, replacing it with its inorder predecessor (the maximum of the left subtree) also keeps the tree a valid BST.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: True. The predecessor is larger than everything else in the left subtree and smaller than everything in the right subtree, so it fits in the deleted node's place. Using the successor instead is symmetric; some implementations alternate between the two to limit skew.

dsa-lists-trees:4.prompt: Inserting the same set of keys into a BST in a different order always produces the same tree shape.
options: True
False
dsa-lists-trees:4.explanation: False. The first key becomes the root and every later key follows comparisons down from there, so order decides the shape. [2,1,3] gives a balanced tree, while [1,2,3] gives a right-leaning chain. The inorder sequence is the same in both cases.
